extracted.intended_audience: federal agency officials, administrative lawyers, and agency rulewriters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for federal agencies on complying with the Administrative Procedure Act's publication, availability, notice, and procedure requirements for organization, procedures, substantive rules, adjudicatory materials, and official records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3 publication requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agency shall separately state and currently publish in the Federal Register its organization, procedures and substantive rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three classes of material — organizational, procedural, and substantive rules — must be published under separate and appropriate headings. Separate statement should not be carried to an extreme that inconveniences the public; cross-references between headings (e.g., procedural notation pointing to substantive rules) are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for functions requiring secrecy in the public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials relating to functions requiring secrecy in the public interest need not be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes confidential operations of agencies (e.g., FBI, Secret Service) and any aspects of law enforcement procedures the disclosure of which would reduce their utility. The exception is only 'to the extent' the function requires secrecy; the agency must determine the scope. Example: military confidential matters need not be published, but ordinary civil functions of the Corps of Engineers must be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for internal management matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Any matter relating solely to the internal management of an agency need not be published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers internal personnel and budget procedures (leaves of absence, vacation, travel). In cases of doubt, agencies are suggested to publish the matter. 'Internal management' also includes internal Federal management functions (e.g., Bureau of the Budget) and interdepartmental committees established by the President.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date / prospective operation of section 3
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3 is prospective in operation (effective September 11, 1946) and does not apply to materials issued prior to that date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previously published procedures need not be republished; appropriate citations to previously published materials are acceptable. Publication is required for substantive rules and policy statements issued on or after the effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate statement: what to include for organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of central and field organization including delegations by the agency of final authority and the established places/methods whereby the public may secure information or make submittals or requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List delegations of final authority by office title (not individual names unless required by law). Do not need to publish ad hoc or isolated delegations. Specify whether opinions issued by field offices are subject to review, list field office locations and functions, and state the types of applications required to be filed with designated offices. State powers exercisable by 'acting' officials where advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of procedures: scope and form
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must state the general course and method by which their functions are channeled and determined, including the nature and requirements of formal or informal procedures, and forms/instructions as to the scope and contents of papers, reports, or examinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish realistic, informative descriptions of procedures for public functions (rulemaking, adjudication, administration of loans/grants/benefits). Agencies need not 'freeze' procedures or invent formalities; they must keep the public currently informed of changes. Emergency/exceptional procedures may be provided for. Where established procedures exist, routing and responsibilities should be stated with reasonable particularity; for infrequent functions, at minimum provide an office to contact. Informal conference procedures should be publicized (how and where to use them). Forms need not be published in full; a statement of function and where copies may be obtained suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: No person required to resort to unpublished organization/procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: No person shall be required to resort to organization or procedure not published under section 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to publish, e.g., a listing of field offices with functions, may support a claim that persons without actual notice are not bound to resort to a field office prior to initiating a case in the central office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive rules: publication of rules and policy statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must publish substantive rules adopted as authorized by law and statements of general policy or interpretations formulated and adopted for the guidance of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exemption for 'rules addressed to and served upon named persons' avoids filling the Federal Register with particularized rulemaking (e.g., schedules of rates). Agencies decide whether to formulate public policy statements; if enunciated in speeches/releases/etc. for public guidance they must be published. Materials intended only for states (not the 'public') need not be published. Statements developed only in adjudicatory orders are not required under section 3(a)(3) but are covered under 3(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(b): availability/publication of opinions and orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Every agency shall publish or make available for public inspection all final opinions or orders in adjudication of cases (except those confidential for good cause) and all rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication need not be in the Federal Register; bound volumes or bulletins suffice. If making materials available for inspection rather than publishing, agencies should publish a rule stating where copies may be obtained and, where practicable, allow inspection in regional as well as central offices. 'Opinions or orders in the adjudication of cases' includes license-related orders. Intermediate orders need not be published unless useful as precedents. Agencies may withhold confidential orders but should provide abstracts showing principles without revealing confidential facts if relying on such materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3(c): official records availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters of official record shall, save as otherwise required by statute, be made available to persons properly and directly concerned, except information held confidential for good cause found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should publish a rule listing types of official records, classify confidentiality, state how information is available (inspection or sale of copies), method of applying, and officials deciding applications. 'Official record' generally includes applications, registrations, petitions, reports filed by the public and documents embodying agency actions (orders, rules, licenses); formal proceeding records (pleadings, transcripts, exhibits) are official. Internal memoranda and intra-agency reports are generally not official records. Agencies determine whether a requester is 'properly and directly concerned.' Confidentiality may be by rule (classes of material) or case-by-case 'for good cause found'; existing statutory confidentiality remains unaffected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of section 4: notice and participation in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 guarantees public opportunity to participate in the rulemaking process: agencies must give public notice of substantive rules they propose to adopt and grant interested persons an opportunity to present views; interested persons also have the right to petition for issuance, amendment or repeal of a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With certain exceptions, no substantive rule may be made effective until at least thirty days after its publication in the Federal Register. Where statute requires rulemaking on the record (sections 7 and 8), those procedures supplant section 4(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4 exceptions (categories exempted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 contains two broad exceptions: (1) any military, naval, or foreign affairs function of the United States; and (2) any matter relating to agency management or personnel or to public property, loans, grants, benefits, or contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign affairs functions are those affecting relations with other governments such that public rulemaking would cause undesirable international consequences; exemption applies broadly (e.g., State Department functions, foreign affairs functions of other agencies). 'Agency management or personnel' aligns with 'internal management' exemptions. 'Public property' covers rules about U.S.-owned real/personal property and trust/guardian property. 'Loans' covers rules about government loans and guarantees. 'Grants' includes subsidy and grant-in-aid programs. 'Benefits' includes veterans pensions, old-age insurance. 'Contracts' covers public contracts and wage determinations made as contract conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(a) notice requirement and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency contemplating a substantive rule subject to section 4(a) must publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register, unless all persons subject are named and personally served or otherwise have actual notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice must include: (1) a statement of the time, place, and nature of public rulemaking proceedings (reasonable notice; plan schedule to allow participation and 30-day pre-effective publication), (2) reference to the authority under which the rule is proposed (sufficiently precise), and (3) either the terms or substance of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved (a description may be used if more informative or to avoid burdening the Register; copies of proposed rule may be made available upon request). The notice should be sufficiently informative to allow intelligent participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of notice for good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may omit the notice (and section 4(b) procedures) if it finds 'for good cause' that notice and public procedure are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency must incorporate in the issued rule its finding of 'good cause' and a brief statement of reasons. 'Impracticable' when due and timely execution would be impeded (e.g., urgent safety rules after accident); 'unnecessary' for minor rules where public interest is minimal; 'contrary to the public interest' when advance notice would defeat rule purpose (e.g., confidential financial controls).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4(b): informal rulemaking procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: For informal rulemaking subject to notice, the agency shall afford interested persons an opportunity to participate through submission of written data, views, or arguments with or without opportunity to present the same orally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency has discretion to choose procedure (written submissions only, informal hearings with/without transcript, conferences, consultation with industry committees, or combinations). Agencies are required to consider 'all relevant matter presented' and are recommended to include an express recital that such material has been considered. Informal rulemaking does not require rules to be based exclusively on the record produced in proceedings; agencies may use materials in files and institutional knowledge in addition to public submissions. Upon completion, the agency must incorporate a 'concise general statement of their basis and purpose' into any adopted rules; elaborate findings of fact/conclusions of law are not required except where statute mandates formal rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal rulemaking where statutes require hearings on the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Where rules are required by statute to be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing, the requirements of sections 7 and 8 apply instead of section 4(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes like the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act require hearings and orders based only on substantial evidence of record and detailed findings of fact; such proceedings begun after section 7/8 effective date must follow formal procedures. Rate- or price-setting statutes commonly require hearings and are treated as requiring decisions on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise general statement of basis and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: After completion of public rulemaking proceedings and 'after consideration of all relevant matter presented,' the agency shall incorporate in any rules adopted a concise general statement of their basis and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement should be 'concise' and 'general' to inform the public and assist courts in interpretation. Except where formal rulemaking is required by statute, findings of fact and conclusions of law are not necessary, nor elaborate analyses of considerations; a general statement suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication/availability of rules addressed to named persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules addressed to and served upon named persons in accordance with law are exempt from section 3(a)(3) publication requirement but are covered by section 3(b) (availability for inspection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids publishing large amounts of particularized rulemaking (e.g., corporate mergers, reorganizations, rate schedules). It is sufficient to make such rules available for public inspection and to publish a rule stating where they may be inspected or obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitional guidance: substantive vs interpretative rules and general policy statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Working definitions: Substantive rule — issued pursuant to statutory authority to implement statute and having force and effect of law. Interpretative rule — advises public of agency's construction of statutes/rules administered. General statement of policy — advises public prospectively of how the agency proposes to exercise discretionary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 4(a) and (b) apply only to substantive rules; interpretative rules, general policy statements, and rules of organization/procedure/practice are exempt from the notice-and-comment requirements unless otherwise required by statute.
